column1: What four musical parameters does standard notation encode, and what does each map to visually?
column2: Pitch (vertical position), Rhythm (horizontal position + notehead shape), Dynamics (letters/symbols like p, f, mf), and Articulation (marks above/below the note).

column1: Why is pitch position on the staff a better mental model than thinking in Hz?
column2: Pitch is logarithmic (doubling frequency = one octave), but the staff always shows the same visual jump of seven lines/spaces per octave — so staff position, not frequency, matches how notation actually works.

column1: What are the line and space mnemonics for Treble clef, and what is the anchor note?
column2: Anchor: G4 on the 2nd line from bottom. Lines (E-G-B-D-F) = 'Every Good Boy Does Fine.' Spaces (F-A-C-E) spell 'FACE.'

column1: What is the anchor note for Bass clef, and why should you avoid translating bass clef through treble clef?
column2: Anchor: F3 on the 4th line from bottom. Translating bass clef through treble clef permanently caps reading speed around 60 BPM — bass clef must be learned as its own language.

column1: What is the practical formula for equal temperament (12-TET), and why does it matter for movable scale shapes?
column2: The octave is divided into 12 equal semitones, each a ratio of 2^(1/12) ≈ 1.05946. This makes every scale/chord shape identical starting from any note, so fretboard patterns and keyboard fingerings are movable to any key.

column1: What single interval (scale degree) determines whether a mode sounds major or minor, and what determines its 'color'?
column2: The 3rd determines major vs. minor. Everything else (2nd, 4th, 6th, 7th) provides color — e.g., Dorian's major 6th vs. Aeolian's minor 6th is the one-semitone difference between 'jazzy minor' and 'sad minor.'

column1: List the seven diatonic modes in order starting from C major's white keys, with their signature characteristic degree.
column2: Ionian (Maj3, Maj7), Dorian (min3, Maj6), Phrygian (♭2, min3), Lydian (Maj3, #4), Mixolydian (Maj3, ♭7), Aeolian (min3, min6, min7), Locrian (♭5).

column1: Why do major triads sound inherently stable from a physics standpoint?
column2: The harmonic series of a single fundamental naturally contains a major triad in its first five partials (f0-f0-2f0(octave)-3f0(5th)-4f0(octave)-5f0(3rd), outlining C-C-G-C-E), so the triad's pitches reinforce each other's overtones instead of creating audible beating.

column1: In functional harmony, what are the three functional zones and which chords belong to each (in a major key)?
column2: Tonic (T): I, vi — home/resolved. Predominant (PD): ii, IV — leaving home, building motion. Dominant (D): V, vii° — maximum tension, demands resolution.

column1: What creates the tension in the V chord, and how does it resolve via voice leading?
column2: The tritone between scale degrees 4 and 7 (F and B in C major) splits the octave evenly, creating instability. It resolves by double half-step motion: the leading tone (B) rises to the tonic (C), and the 4th (F) falls to the 3rd (E).

column1: What two voice-leading errors should be avoided, and what is the rule for resolving tendency tones?
column2: Avoid parallel fifths and parallel octaves (voices moving in lockstep lose independence and sound hollow). Resolve tendency tones by step: leading tone up to tonic, chordal 7th down to the 3rd of the next chord.

column1: What are the three invariants underlying musical form (e.g., sonata form), per the performer's model of listening?
column2: 1) Tonal departure and return (leaving and returning to home key). 2) Multi-timescale tension (phrase, section, and movement resolutions coordinated, not all at once). 3) Identity vs. transformation (thematic material stays recognizable while changing).
